item.title: USA Today Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Use of News Articles
item.description:
USA Today Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Use of News Articles

USA Today Co has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that the company used the publisher’s copyrighted articles without permission.

🏛️ Overview

  • The complaint states that OpenAI copied hundreds of thousands of articles and other materials belonging to USA Today Co for AI training.
  • The lawsuit seeks damages exceeding $250 million and an injunction to stop the alleged infringement.

📄 Claims and Demands

  • USA Today claims the material was used without permission.
  • The company is demanding over $250 million in damages and seeks a court order to prevent further use.
  • The complaint does not settle whether OpenAI is legally obligated to pay for any alleged use.

⚖️ Legal Issues

  • The central question is whether OpenAI’s use of the articles violates copyright or falls under fair use.
  • Fair use is a US copyright doctrine that permits use of copyrighted material without prior permission under certain conditions.
  • AI firms argue that training models is a fair‑use activity because the system learns patterns and generates new output.
  • Publishers dispute this, asserting that large‑scale copying should not be deemed legal.
  • Courts consider four factors:
    1. Purpose of the use
    2. Character of the copyrighted work
    3. Amount and substantiality of the portion used
    4. Effect on the market value of the original work
  • Additional considerations may include whether the use is sufficiently transformative, the commercial context, and the impact on the publisher’s ability to profit from its reporting.

📈 Potential Impact

  • The decision could shape how AI companies collect and use news articles in the future.
  • The case adds to a broader legal debate about applying existing copyright rules to generative AI.
  • Similar lawsuits have been filed by other news organizations, including The New York Times, against OpenAI and Microsoft.

📰 Industry Concerns

  • Publishers rely on revenue from advertisements, subscriptions, and licensing.
  • There is concern that AI products could use content without paying, potentially reducing publishers’ income.
  • AI‑generated answers might keep users from visiting the original news site, further impacting revenue.
  • Licensing agreements are presented as one way for AI developers to obtain commercial access to news content.

#OpenAI #CopyrightLaw #NewsIndustry #AIlitigation

Source: USA Today sues OpenAI: USA Today vs OpenAI: Key questions over ChatGPT training data, news copyright and whether publishers should be paid for their work - The Economic Times

item.title: USA Today Sues OpenAI for Over $250 Million Over Copyright Infringement
item.description:
USA Today Sues OpenAI for Over $250 Million Over Copyright Infringement

USA Today Co., together with several local newspapers it owns, has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI alleging that the AI company copied “hundreds of thousands” of articles to train its models.

🔍 Overview

  • USA Today is the latest publisher to sue OpenAI.
  • The lawsuit seeks damages of more than $250 million.
  • The filing claims OpenAI’s use of the content has caused “real and continuing” harm to the outlets.

⚖️ Legal Claims

  • OpenAI allegedly did not ask for permission to use USA Today’s articles.
  • The plaintiff asserts OpenAI “took” the content to build products worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
  • The complaint states that OpenAI’s commercial success rests on large‑scale copyright infringement.
  • The core allegation is that OpenAI copied hundreds of thousands of articles for training its AI models.

📄 Parties Involved

  • Plaintiff: USA Today Co. (including its local newspapers)
  • Local outlets named in the suit: The Tennessean, Indy Star, The Columbus Dispatch, The Oklahoman, and several others.
  • Other publishers currently suing OpenAI:
    • The New York Times
    • The Intercept
    • CNET owner Ziff Davis
    • CBC/Radio‑Canada
    • Encyclopaedia Britannica
    • Merriam‑Webster
    • The Seattle Times
    • A coalition of nearly 400 local newspapers

📈 Why It Matters

  • The case adds to a growing string of copyright lawsuits against OpenAI.
  • Plaintiffs argue that the alleged infringement harms the news industry’s ability to monetize content.
  • OpenAI has not responded to a request for comment from The Verge.

The outcome could influence how AI developers source and use copyrighted material.

#OpenAI #CopyrightLaw #MediaLawsuits

Source: USA Today becomes the latest publisher to sue OpenAI

item.title: Trump Administration Intervenes in New York Times Copyright Lawsuit Supporting OpenAI
item.description:
Trump Administration Intervenes in New York Times Copyright Lawsuit Supporting OpenAI

The Trump administration has intervened in The New York Times’ copyright lawsuit against OpenAI, filing a statement of interest in favor of the artificial intelligence laboratory. The administration is supporting OpenAI’s argument that training AI models on copyrighted text constitutes fair use, asserting that letting models train on copyrighted work will preserve American prosperity.

⚖️ The Government’s Statement of Interest

In the newly filed statement of interest, US attorneys argued that restricting AI development would conflict with basic legal frameworks. Key assertions in the filing include:

  • Narrowing Fair Use: US attorneys wrote that “The New York Times seeks to narrow fair-use doctrine to exclude the training of OpenAI’s large language models (LLMs).”
  • Hampering Progress: The filing stated that “That result would be inconsistent with basic copyright law principles and severely hamper ‘the Progress of Science and useful Arts.’”
  • Scientific Breakthroughs: The attorneys wrote that “LLMs are already helping researchers across fields achieve major breakthroughs.”
  • Economic Impact: The administration warned that “constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”
  • The Fair Use Standard: While the attorneys noted that “The fair-use inquiry hinges on the specific facts and uses at issue in each case,” they argued that “it would be problematic — and legally incorrect — to impose broad copyright liability that would generally render training of AI models impermissible without licensing.” They concluded that LLM training is “consistent with that creative ‘progress’ that is the basic constitutional objective of copyright itself.”

🔍 Background on the Lawsuit

Originally filed in December 2023, the landmark lawsuit alleges that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI systems on articles from The New York Times. The media outlet is seeking “billions of dollars” in damages from both OpenAI and Microsoft.

This case has major implications, as it could set a precedent for other media companies concerned about AI systems training on their work. Copyright disagreements between media outlets and AI firms have intensified in recent years, leading to other active lawsuits from the Center for Investigative Reporting, Chicago Tribune, and New York Daily News.

🧩 Policy and Legal Context

To advance its policy objectives, the Trump administration has leaned heavily on filing statements of interest in private litigation—a strategy that one official has described as “incredibly” successful. The administration has previously made the case that AI training should count as fair use in its National AI Legislative Framework.

Additionally, Donald Trump holds a personal animus toward The New York Times, against which he is currently pursuing an active defamation lawsuit.

🤝 Industry Precedents and Licensing

While the New York Times litigation continues, the broader AI and media landscape has seen a mixture of licensing agreements and high-stakes legal outcomes.

Entity Action Details
OpenAI Licensing Deals Has signed content licensing agreements with dozens of media outlets, including The Associated Press, Axel Springer, and Vox Media.
Amazon Licensing Deal (2025) Entered into an agreement with The New York Times allowing the publisher’s editorial content, including news articles and recipes, to appear in Amazon’s generative AI tools.
Anthropic Legal Settlement (2025) Resolved a dispute with a $1.5 billion settlement with authors. A judge ruled Anthropic could legally train models on lawfully purchased books, but could still be held liable for piracy.

#OpenAI #FairUse #CopyrightLaw #TrumpAdministration #NewYorkTimes

Source: The Trump administration is supporting OpenAI in the NYT copyright lawsuit
